title: Midterm Senate races spotlight data centres, crypto spending and Trump influence
text: Midterm Senate races spotlight data centres, crypto spending and Trump influence Seven key Senate battles are being shaped by record spending, crypto industry money and a growing backlash against data centres, with President Donald Trump's popularity under scrutiny in the most expensive midterm cycle in US history. A growing backlash against data centres has become a defining issue in seven key Senate races across the United States, as political integrity and the popularity of President Donald Trump come under scrutiny in the most expensive midterm election cycle in US history. The so-called techlash is real among Republicans and Democrats in both cities and the countryside. The Brookings Institution says it could have momentous ramifications for everyone. If several high-profile backers of data centres lose and their opponents win, it could encourage politicians to embrace more data centre moratoriums, pauses and audits, creating financial difficulties not only for specific firms but for the overall economy.Data Centre Backlash In Senate RacesIn Pennsylvania, Republican candidate Stacy Garrity has accused Democrat Josh Shapiro of opening the state's door to data centres and giving away state tax dollars and resources to a company, Amazon, on the other side of the country. The race is one of several where the techlash could shift outcomes. In Alaska, surging heating fuel, electricity and grocery prices are disproportionately whacking residents of the remote, traditionally red state.The race between Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola has turned particularly bitter. The Trump administration's Department of Justice last week filed a lawsuit requesting Alaska not to certify its Senate results if Peltola wins, arguing that having two Dan Sullivans on the ballot threatened the integrity of the vote count. Peltola retorted that the bid raised profound constitutional concerns.Iowa is something of a case study on the popularity of Trump, who has asked voters to pretend he is on the ballot despite his weakened approval rating. Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek are locked in a tight battle for the US Senate seat. Traditionally red Iowa could be on the cusp of turning blue, with Turek neck and neck with the self-described common-sense mum Hinson.Inflation And War Impact CampaignsInflation is hitting the state hard, and Hinson has been recorded asking supporters to donate gas money for her campaign bus. After voting in favour of the Iran war, Hinson has since criticised the president's decision to buy oil from Russia and stated that a vote for her is not necessarily a vote for the president. I do want to see the war come to an end as soon as possible, she told NBC.A vote for me is a vote for Iowa. Turek, a former Paralympian born with spina bifida, says if elected he will push for an end to the Iran war and the repeal of Trump's widespread tariffs, but has no interest in voting to impeach the president. In Texas, James Talarico is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from the conservative state since 1988. He has built his campaign around concerns about political corruption.This is a people-powered movement to take on this broken, corrupt political system, Talarico has told supporters. We are a threat to their corrupt system. Elon Musk has ploughed hundreds of millions into Republican campaigns this cycle. That included payments of US$75 million on September 9 and US$83 million on September 23 to the Senate Leadership Fund PAC, which were transferred the next day to the campaign of the state's attorney-general.Crypto Spending Targets Senate ContendersElon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat, said Talarico, whom Trump likes to refer to as Talafreako. There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US senator. The Trump family has made a motza from cryptocurrency, and the crypto industry has poured US$176 million into promoting allies in these midterms, Reuters reports.In Ohio, former senator Sherrod Brown chaired the Senate banking committee from 2021 to 2024, when he was a vocal critic of crypto. Ad-tracking business AdImpact says the crypto sector has spent US$68 million on defeating Brown, who is up against Republican incumbent Jon Husted. An ad featuring Donna Arthur, the estranged mother of candidate Acton, called her daughter a lifelong liar despite having had no contact with her for nearly 50 years.Arthur lost custody of her children in 1978 after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12. The ad was widely seen as having crossed an ethical line, and even several prominent Republicans called for it to be taken down. Trump had encouraged Ramaswamy to keep airing the ad, saying it was hitting pay dirt. Ramaswamy said during a campaign appearance in Ohio on Thursday that the ad's planned run was over.Michigan Race Features Religious RhetoricIn Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a doctor, unionist and Muslim, and Republican Mike Rogers are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democrat Gary Peters. El-Sayed has galvanised young voters but has faced anti-Muslim rhetoric from Trump, who delights in calling him Mohamed. After a bitter primary, some Democrats have refused to support him over his criticism of Israel, past remarks and association with controversial podcaster Hasan Piker.The progressive Democrat believes he is being targeted because he is Muslim, and calls it out. Trump has seized on this, labelling it arrogance. He's a nasty guy, he's worse than I am, Trump recently said. Trump's trade stoush with Canada and high petrol prices due to the Iran war are deeply unpopular in Michigan, but it may be the Republicans' best chance to flip a seat in a state that has not elected a GOP senator in decades.
summary: A growing backlash against data centres has become a defining issue in seven key Senate races across the United States, as political integrity and the popularity of President Donald Trump come under scrutiny in the most expensive midterm election cycle in US history. In Alaska, surging heating fuel, electricity and grocery prices are disproportionately whacking residents of the remote, traditionally red state.The race between Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola has turned particularly bitter.
